description.summary: The Púca is a shapeshifting fairy creature of Irish, Welsh, Cornish, Manx, and Scottish Gaelic folklore — most famously a black horse with luminous golden eyes. Its character is ambiguous: it can be a dangerous trickster or a beneficent helper, and is closely associated with Samhain (1 November).
description.full: The Púca (Irish, often anglicised as Pooka or Phouka; Welsh Pwca; Cornish Bucca; Manx Phynnodderee in some treatments; Scottish Gaelic Bòcan) is a Celtic spirit and one of the most prominent figures of Irish fairy belief. It is fundamentally a shapeshifter, taking the form of a black horse, goat, hare, dog, bull, eagle, or human (sometimes with animal ears or a tail) and appearing on remote roads at night. The horse-form Púca is the most famous: a black or dark-coated stallion with glowing golden eyes that may invite or seize a human rider for a wild, terrifying ride before depositing them, often unhurt, in the morning. The Púca's moral character is famously ambiguous — it is mischievous, occasionally malicious, but can also speak in a human voice, give cryptic advice, and even perform helpful labour for those who treat it well. It is associated above all with Samhain (1 November / Lá na Púca), the date after which any wild fruit not yet harvested is said to belong to the Púca and may not be eaten by humans. Iron and references to the saints are traditional defenses. Cognate figures include the Welsh Pwca, the Cornish Bucca, and Shakespeare's Puck (Robin Goodfellow), all sharing the same Common Brittonic / Old English etymological root.

etymology.origin: Old Irish púca, cognate with Welsh pwca, Cornish bucca, Old English pūca; further cognates appear in Old Norse púki ('devil, imp') and Middle English pouke
etymology.meaning: Glossed in Irish lexicons as 'spirit, ghost, hobgoblin, goblin'; the cluster of cognates carries the sense 'mischievous spirit'
etymology.first_use: Old Irish attestations in early medieval Irish texts; English 'pooka' / 'phouka' from at least the 17th century

taxonomy.variant: Celtic (Irish, Welsh, Cornish, Manx, Scottish Gaelic)

features.description: Takes a variety of forms — black horse, goat, hare, dog, bull, eagle, or human (often with animal ears or tail)
Particularly the horse-form Púca is described with glowing golden or fiery eyes
Horse-form Púca has a long, often unkempt mane
Can speak in a human voice, giving advice, warnings, or prophecy

physical.morphology: Inherently protean. Most accounts agree on a base of a large dark animal — most often a horse — with uncanny features (glowing eyes, exceptional size, eloquent speech).

abilities.description: Changes form at will between several animal and human shapes
Lures or seizes a person onto its back as a horse and gallops over impassable terrain before releasing them
Speaks intelligibly to humans and is sometimes consulted for cryptic advice
In some Munster traditions, will perform farm labour at night for households that treat it respectfully
After Samhain, the Púca is said to spoil or spit on uncollected blackberries and fruit so that humans may not eat them

behavior.diet: Said to spoil and consume wild fruit after Samhain; otherwise not specified
patterns: Most active around Samhain (Lá na Púca, 1 November)
Encounters typically at night on lonely roads
Either tricks or aids individual humans depending on their conduct
Repelled by iron and by appeals to the saints

range.description: The Púca and its direct cognates are found across the Celtic fringe of the British Isles and Ireland, with the strongest tradition in Ireland (especially Munster, Leinster, and parts of Connacht), and counterparts in Wales (Pwca), Cornwall (Bucca), and the Scottish Highlands (Bòcan).

temporal.seasonal_patterns: Most active around Samhain (1 November); the night of 31 October to 1 November is associated with the Púca's wild rides and the spoiling of wild fruit.

origins.cultural_roots: Rooted in pre-Christian Celtic supernatural belief and the broader Indo-European 'mischievous spirit' / hobgoblin complex, surviving into Christian-era Irish, Welsh, Cornish, and Scottish folklore.
origins.earliest_accounts: Attested in Old Irish texts and lexicons as a generic term for hobgoblins and ghosts; the proper-name fairy figure crystallises in early modern Irish oral tradition.
origins.folklore_connections: Cognate figures appear in English (Puck, Robin Goodfellow), Welsh (Pwca), Cornish (Bucca), Scottish Gaelic (Bòcan), and Old Norse (púki). The horse-form Púca is closely related to but distinct from the Scottish kelpie and each-uisge.

history.modern_era: Púca traditions remain widely known in Ireland and the wider Celtic diaspora. Samhain customs, including the prohibition on picking blackberries after 1 November, continue to be cited in folkloric and popular sources. Literary and screen treatments have kept the figure prominent: Mary Chase's 1944 play Harvey, the 1950 James Stewart film of the same name, and recent animated and television adaptations such as Hilda all draw on the Púca/Pooka tradition.

notable.name: Samhain blackberry tradition (Lá na Púca)

types: Folklore informants collected by Yeats and Lady Wilde

notable.description: Across Ireland, after 1 November (Lá na Púca / Samhain), wild blackberries and other fruit are traditionally said to belong to the Púca, who has spat on or otherwise spoiled them, and may not be eaten. The tradition is widely attested in 19th- and 20th-century folklore collections.

credibility.notes: Treated as living folklore rather than a paranormal sighting.

sources: Yeats, W. B. (1888), Fairy and Folk Tales of the Irish Peasantry

notable.name: Pwca of Cwm Pwca (Welsh tradition)
notable.description: Nineteenth-century Welsh antiquarian sources record the Pwca of Cwm Pwca, a glen near Crickhowell, as the local hobgoblin who would lead travellers astray with a will-o'-the-wisp light before vanishing with mocking laughter.

factors: Recorded multiple times in 19th-century Welsh folklore

paranormal.name: Living Celtic fairy
paranormal.description: Within the tradition itself, the Púca is treated as a real, intentional fairy being whose presence demands ritual respect, especially at Samhain.
proponents: Modern revivalist Pagan and Druidic communities

skeptical.name: Folkloric and literary tradition
skeptical.description: Folklorists treat the Púca as a culturally specific personification of liminal danger and harvest-end risk rather than a literal entity.
evidence_cited: Functional fit with Samhain seasonal transitions

skeptical.name: Misidentification of nocturnal animals
skeptical.description: Some sceptical commentators have suggested that horse-form Púca encounters reflect misidentified loose horses, deer, or shadows on rural roads at night.
evidence_cited: Common Irish nocturnal megafauna and visibility conditions

folklore.beliefs: Within Irish tradition, the Púca is at once a danger and a source of cryptic guidance; respectful behaviour towards it is rewarded, disrespect punished.

indigenous.significance: Among the most widely recognised figures of Celtic fairy belief, integral to harvest customs and Samhain.
indigenous.sensitivity_note: Care should be taken to distinguish living Irish-language traditions from Anglophone literary appropriations such as Shakespeare's Puck.
indigenous.respect_guidelines: Cite Irish-language sources and the Schools' Collection of the Irish Folklore Commission where possible; avoid conflating distinct cognate figures.
